Table 4. Final α=0.50 lists: mean popularity counts distinct positive-training users; overlap compares the two users within a method.

| Method | User 1 mean popularity | User 2 mean popularity | Shared movies / 10 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Popularity | 246.8 | 262.1 | 1 |
| Global PageRank | 239.4 | 247.4 | 1 |
| PPR | 228.4 | 226.7 | 1 |
| Standalone MF | 99.1 | 79.9 | 4 |

The [eight complete Top-10 lists](results/users_1_2/index.html) and [80-row CSV](results/users_1_2/recommendations.csv) include every ID, title, genres, score, training popularity and known test rating; unknown remains unobserved. For user 1, PPR starts with *Fargo* (Crime, Drama, Thriller), whereas MF starts with *The Wrong Trousers* (Animation, Comedy). For user 2, PPR starts with *Return of the Jedi* (Action, Adventure, Romance, Sci-Fi, War), whereas MF starts with *Persuasion* (Romance). These differences do not establish preference fit: user 2 has no Top-10 hits under any method. Both users receive ten positive-score candidates in all four methods.

Table 5. Required demonstrations, separate from final evaluation. All settings use the same training graph and standard per-user test filtering.

| Setting | User | α | Mean popularity | Overlap with setting 1 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1 | 0.85 | 245.5 | — |
| 2 | 2 | 0.85 | 254.9 | 0/10 |
| 3 | 1 | 0.50 | 228.4 | 7/10 |

Settings 1→2 change user at α=0.85: zero overlap, with mean popularity 245.5→254.9. All ten user-2 recommendations were already rated by user 1, and six user-1 recommendations were excluded for user 2, so the difference includes user-specific filtering. Settings 1→3 hold user 1 and exclusions fixed and lower α from 0.85 to 0.50: seven shared movies, mean popularity 245.5→228.4. *Scream*, *Air Force One* and *Titanic* leave; *Trainspotting*, *Sense and Sensibility* and *E.T.* enter. Here higher α gives the more popular list; no universal novelty or quality improvement follows. [Three full lists and comparisons](results/ppr_demonstration/index.html).

### 4.3 Worked numerical verification for user 1 and Fargo

**Setup.**

For movie 100 at α=0.50, the original 32-column WebGL batch and a read-only observed copy were run on the same graph. User 1 maps to node 0; Fargo to node 1042, with 377 positive-training neighbours. The last update is iteration 21, residual 9.95331675×10⁻⁷. Incoming mass is the Float32 matrix reduction of neighbour probabilities divided across their degrees. Restart is at user 1, so Fargo’s restart entry is zero; total dangling mass is also zero. Sources: [graph.js:656](graph.js#L656) through its restart update, and [graphCorrectPartitionMass(), graph.js:730](graph.js#L730).

**Results.**

Table 6. Measured final-step values.

| Final-iteration value | Actual output |
| --- | --- |
| Incoming mass at Fargo | 0.0013710429193452 |
| Dangling / restart contribution at Fargo | 0 / 0 |
| Raw Fargo score = 0.50 × incoming | 0.0006855214596726 |
| Raw movie-partition sum | 0.3333335220813751 |
| Target movie-partition mass | 0.33333349227905273 |
| Final normalized Fargo score | 0.0006855214014649391 |
| Difference from saved score | 0 |

The actual correction is Float32(Float32(raw / 0.3333335220813751) × 0.33333349227905273), giving exactly **0.0006855214014649391**, the saved score. It lowers raw by 5.82076609×10⁻¹¹. The finite-iteration user target is (1+α(−α)ᵗ)/(1+α); movie target is its complement. The observed and original solver outputs match exactly across all 32 probability columns. A separate Float64 iteration gives 0.000685520996303016, a −4.05161923×10⁻¹⁰ precision difference, disclosed rather than substituted for the production value.

Fargo is in the training candidate pool but absent from user 1’s training and validation histories. It ranks first among 1,367 eligible candidates; its held-out rating is 5 ([u.data:17673](u.data#L17673)). All three Top-10 hits are:

| Rank | Movie ID | Top-10 hit | Test rating |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 100 | Fargo (1996) | 5 |
| 2 | 258 | Contact (1997) | 5 |
| 7 | 222 | Star Trek: First Contact (1996) | 4 |

User 1 has **19 eligible relevant test movies**, with IDs 6, 18, 20, 32, 100, 111, 129, 154, 169, 171, 178, 209, 221, 222, 228, 242, 256, 258 and 270; the other nine test ratings are below 4. Thus individual **Recall@10 = 3/19 = 0.1578947368**, distinct from the cohort average. [Complete explanation](results/user1_fargo_worked/index.html), [19-item audit](results/user1_fargo_worked/eligible_relevant_test_movies.csv) and [machine-readable vectors and contributions](results/user1_fargo_worked/intermediates.json) preserve exact values, source lines and numerical-rounding differences.

### 4.4 Verification coverage

**Setup.**

The post-fix harness covers reference vectors, normalized rows, restart validity, mass/nonnegativity, matrix orientation, dangling nodes, mapped seeds, caps, repeat-run memory, candidate filtering, macro recall, batched parity and the MF-loss regression. Sources: `runSelfChecks()` and `hw6CheckBatchedPpr()` in `script.js`.

**Results.**

The preserved run has **21 PASS, 0 FAIL, 0 PENDING** ([verification.json](results/final_evaluation/verification.json)); it is not presented as a new harness execution during report drafting. Twelve batch user/α fixture cases match single-user PPR; dangling restart and cleanup pass. Six propagation runs retain 2/2 live tensors in the MF-loaded harness; the separate Fargo trace has 0/0. All four validation sweeps converge within the cap. Checks establish implementation consistency, not user satisfaction or cold-start performance.

## 5. Discussion

**Failure case.**

MF originally produced nearly identical predictions close to μ and poorly distinguished users and movies. The saved [failure record](results/mf_root_cause.json) preserves this observed symptom; no fabricated before/after benchmark is supplied.

**Root cause.**

MSE was averaged over the current mini-batch, while L2 was summed over every user and movie factor on every batch. At the configured coefficient, this scale imbalance suppressed factor learning, including factors unrelated to the current observations.

**Fix and verification.**

The loss now averages the squared norms of the user/movie rows gathered for current-batch observations: mean_batch(error²)+0.05·mean_batch(||pᵤ||²+||qᵢ||²), retaining repeated-observation weights. `hw6MfBatchLoss()` ([script.js:837](script.js#L837)) and its regression check show that unrelated rows neither change the loss nor receive gradients. The post-fix harness passes 21/0/0; epoch 4 is selected by validation RMSE. The retrieval comparison uses this corrected model, not the older collapsed model.

**What worked.**

- PPR has the highest observed common-cohort Recall@10, while the fixed-user and Fargo audits verify filtering and score interpretation.
- A lower α improves validation retrieval in this grid; the controlled user-1 example also reduces mean popularity, without proving that less popular recommendations are better.

**Draft deployment interpretation for student review.** Replace the current MF baseline with PPR for the warm-user Top-10 surface, subject to an online test; this conclusion applies to this baseline and protocol, not all MF systems. Pair lists, multi-genre histories and popularity describe output differences, while cohort recall supplies the retrieval comparison. The per-user split, static explicit ratings and warm cohort cannot establish current-session intent, completion, retention, revenue or cold-start performance.

Before rollout, assign accounts persistently to MF control or PPR α=0.50 treatment, keeping interface, exposure and eligibility rules fixed. The proposed primary outcome is the fraction of exposed users starting a recommended movie and watching at least ten minutes within 24 hours; guardrails are total watch time per exposed user and p95 recommendation latency. Analyze at the assigned-user level without switching arms between sessions, and set the observation window and decision rule before examining results.

**What surprised me or did not work.**

- **Draft reflection, not yet student-confirmed:** fixing the loss made predictions distinguishable, but MF still had the lowest retrieval recall; improving an MSE-based learner does not guarantee better Top-10 ranking.
- Zero overlap for the two α=0.85 users is partly explained by exclusions. Neither that overlap nor the lower mean popularity of MF’s lists demonstrates superior personalization or discovery.

## 6. AI Usage Disclosure

- **AI tools used:** OpenAI Codex, including browser/terminal tools and a reference-verification sub-agent; exact model/build was not recorded.
- **How AI was used:** AI assisted data preparation, graph/propagation and retrieval implementation, MF debugging, numerical tracing, literature verification and report drafting; saved JSON/CSV artifacts preserve the outputs used here.
- **What I personally verified:** Not confirmed. The harness, independent calculations and Fargo worksheet were run by the agent; this draft does not attribute them to the student.
- **What I trusted without full verification:** Student statement pending; the title-block identity/contact fields are explicitly mocked at the user’s request. No claim that all AI outputs were personally checked is made.
- **Session log reference:** The required unmodified tool-native `student_hw6_session.json` has not been supplied. No synthetic session file was created. The current submission directory/deadline and continuing session-export requirement also need instructor confirmation; this is a review draft, not a submission-ready bundle.


## References

# Personalized PageRank for MovieLens Top 10 Retrieval

**Student:** Raimova Alina  
**Team:** Individual  
**Email:** aaraimova@edu.hse.ru
**Date:** 2026-10-27  
**Assignment:** Graph-Based Recommendations with Personalized PageRank (Week 6, HW6)
**Github link:** [MOCK — repository URL to add]

## Abstract

This study tests whether Personalized PageRank can improve warm-user movie retrieval over popularity, global PageRank, and a matrix-factorization baseline on MovieLens 100K. The protocol uses 79,619 training, 9,596 validation, and 10,785 test ratings, mean training rating μ = 3.58060262, and popularity Recall@10 = 0.07602291. With alpha selected on validation, PPR reaches test Recall@10 of 0.11218853 across 861 common users, compared with 0.03124894 for the corrected MF baseline. These offline results support testing PPR as the warm-user Top-10 recommender, while leaving viewing and business outcomes to a user-level online experiment.

**Index Terms -** personalized PageRank, movie recommendation, matrix factorization, retrieval evaluation

## 1. Introduction

**Problem statement.**

The task ranks eligible unseen movies from explicit MovieLens ratings while treating missing entries as unobserved. It compares graph walks with popularity and the current standalone MF baseline under one shared retrieval protocol.

**Motivation.**

A rating predictor can have useful RMSE yet retrieve few held-out relevant movies. A consistent candidate pool, exclusion rule and warm-user cohort are therefore needed before choosing a Top-10 recommender.

**Concrete example.**

For user 1, Fargo was not rated in training or validation, so it can be recommended. The worked example traces its PPR score through normalization and checks its held-out rating of 5.

**Contributions.**

- Implement and verify TensorFlow.js PageRank/PPR, including equal outgoing probabilities, personal restart and dangling-mass preservation.
- Compare four methods with validation-selected settings, retain fixed-user evidence, and diagnose the MF regularization defect with a regression check.

## 2. Related Work

MovieLens documents explicit ratings and rating timestamps [1]. PageRank aggregates incoming link mass after dividing each source’s mass among its outgoing links [2]; personalized restart biases this process toward selected nodes [3]. MF estimates observed ratings using latent-factor interactions and regularization [4]. TensorFlow.js supplies the tensor operations and explicit memory management used here [5].

[1] F. M. Harper and J. A. Konstan, “The MovieLens Datasets: History and Context,” *ACM Transactions on Interactive Intelligent Systems*, vol. 5, no. 4, Art. 19, 2015, doi: 10.1145/2827872. [Publication record](https://experts.umn.edu/en/publications/the-movielens-datasets-history-and-context/); [official 100K README](https://files.grouplens.org/datasets/movielens/ml-100k/README). Accessed: Oct. 27, 2026.

[2] L. Page, S. Brin, R. Motwani, and T. Winograd, “The PageRank Citation Ranking: Bringing Order to the Web,” Stanford InfoLab, Technical Report, 1999. [Archived Stanford record](https://web.archive.org/web/20091118014915/http:/ilpubs.stanford.edu:8090/422/); [early draft dated Jan. 29, 1998](https://cs.brown.edu/courses/csci2531/papers/pagerank.pdf). Accessed: Oct. 27, 2026.

[3] G. Jeh and J. Widom, “Scaling personalized web search,” in *Proc. 12th Int. Conf. World Wide Web*, 2003, pp. 271–279, doi: 10.1145/775152.775191. [Conference full text](https://areto.ethz.ch/CDstore/www2003/papers/refereed/p185/html/p185-jeh.html). Accessed: Oct. 27, 2026.

[4] Y. Koren, R. Bell, and C. Volinsky, “Matrix Factorization Techniques for Recommender Systems,” *Computer*, vol. 42, no. 8, 2009, doi: 10.1109/MC.2009.263. [Primary article](https://www.cs.columbia.edu/~blei/fogm/readings/KorenBellVolinsky2009.pdf). Accessed: Oct. 27, 2026.

[5] TensorFlow, “Tensors and operations,” *TensorFlow.js Guide*, and “TensorFlow.js API, version 4.22.0.” [Tensor guide](https://www.tensorflow.org/js/guide/tensors_operations); [versioned API](https://js.tensorflow.org/api/4.22.0/#tidy). Accessed: Oct. 27, 2026.

**Alternatives considered.**

- **Popularity and global PageRank:** retain transparent, nonpersonal baselines; global scores still receive each user’s exclusions.
- **MF:** retain an observed-rating latent-factor comparator; its checkpoint objective is rating error, unlike PPR’s retrieval objective.

## 3. Method

**Approach.**

Popularity counts distinct users with a training rating ≥4 per movie. Construct a binary bidirectional user–movie graph from those positive ratings. For nonzero-degree nodes, Q divides outgoing mass by degree; zero-degree rows remain zero. Iterate p₀=v and p(t+1)=α(Qᵀp(t)+d(t)v)+(1−α)v, where d(t) is dangling mass. Global PageRank uses uniform v; PPR uses one-hot restart at the target user, with α the link-following probability.

**Pipeline.**

1. Load `u.data` and Latin-1 `u.item`; split per user with `data.js`.
2. Build contiguous training-ID mappings and the positive graph; propagate with `R` and `Rᵀ` matrix blocks.
3. Select shared α on validation; restore MF’s validation-RMSE checkpoint.
4. Rank eligible training-movie candidates and evaluate the same test users.

**Tools and libraries.**

- TensorFlow.js **4.22.0**, **WebGL**, Float32: batched propagation and MF [5]; d3 **7.9.0**: graph display only. Python **3.12.14** and NumPy **2.3.5** provide independent numerical audits.
- `tf.tidy()` scopes synchronous steps; retained tensors are disposed. `dataSync()` readback and cooperative yields are used because asynchronous readback stalled this app; no async callback is placed inside `tidy`. Exact GPU/browser build and algorithm-only wall times were not recorded, so no speed benchmark is claimed.

**Key design decisions.**

- **Training-only graph:** 943 users + 1,611 movies = 2,554 nodes; 45,602 positive edges, one zero-degree user and 253 zero-degree movies. No graph/candidate padding node is added; low ratings are observed exclusions, not positive edges or missing zero targets.
- **Mass and convergence:** stop at L1 residual <10⁻⁶ or 500 iterations; report caps honestly. The batch width is 32, with columns frozen independently. Positive-user PPR corrects Float32 partition drift using analytically known finite-iteration user/movie totals before measuring residual.

**Configuration.**

Table 1. Data and popularity baseline, before model metrics; [full provenance](results/report_preamble.json).

| Required pre-model quantity | Value | Calculation source and settings |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Train / validation / test ratings | 79,619 / 9,596 / 10,785 | [data.js:145](data.js#L145), `splitByTimestamp()`; per-user floor(80%)/floor(10%)/remainder, timestamp then movie ID, minimum 5 ratings |
| μ, mean training rating | 3.58060261998 = 285,084 / 79,619 | [script.js:948](script.js#L948), mean inside `hw6TrainMf()`; all observed training ratings 1–5 only |
| Popularity baseline TEST Recall@10 | 0.07602291344 | [script.js:1250](script.js#L1250), `recallAtK("popularity",10,"test")`; 861 users, 1,611 candidates, relevance ≥4, training+validation exclusions |

The loaded data contain 100,000 ratings, 943 users and 1,682 metadata movies. Sparsity over the unpadded observed-ID rectangle is 93.6953%; training contains only 1,611 movies. No users are skipped at splitting. This is per-user chronological, not globally time-consistent; rating times are not viewing sessions.

MF scores are μ+pᵤᵀqᵢ, with 16 factors, seed 20261013, Adam learning rate 0.01, batch size 512, 30 epochs and L2 coefficient 0.05. Missing pairs are not rating targets. No completed Week-5 checkpoint is available, so this is an explicitly disclosed standalone-baseline deviation from the requested reuse. PPR has no optimizer or random seed; α∈{0.50,0.70,0.85,0.95} is selected on validation only. Scores are walk probabilities, not ratings or purchase probabilities, and are not comparable in scale with MF. Run: from `week6`, execute `python3 -m http.server 8000`, open `http://localhost:8000/index.html`, then use “Evaluate Recall@10 — all four methods”; the separate two-user demo is not part of that evaluation.

## 4. Experiments

### 4.1 Validation selection and final shared-cohort evaluation

**Setup.**

The candidate pool contains all 1,611 training movies. Validation excludes training-rated movies; test excludes every training- or validation-rated movie regardless of rating. Relevant items have evaluation rating ≥4 and remain eligible. Sort descending by score, breaking exact ties by ascending movie ID. Recall@10 is the macro-average of each user’s hits divided by eligible relevant items. Warm users need a positive training edge, scoreable MF candidates and eligible relevant held-out items. Validation has 846 users; test has 861 of 943. The 82 users without eligible relevant test items include the one zero-positive-edge user; these counts overlap. Thirteen relevant test observations are outside the candidate pool. Validation excludes 97 users without eligible relevance and four out-of-pool relevant observations.

**Results.**

Table 2. PPR validation selection; α = 0.50 wins, with exact ties assigned to the smaller α.

| α | Validation Recall@10 | Max iterations | All converged |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0.50 | 0.11448316 | 22 | yes |
| 0.70 | 0.10479695 | 42 | yes |
| 0.85 | 0.09002077 | 92 | yes |
| 0.95 | 0.07375030 | 287 | yes |

Table 3. Final TEST results on the same 861 users. The selected α also controls global PageRank; it was not separately optimized for PageRank.

| Method | α | Test Recall@10 | Mean training popularity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Popularity | — | 0.07602291 | 272.00 |
| Global PageRank | 0.50 | 0.07969324 | 257.82 |
| PPR | 0.50 | 0.11218853 | 244.21 |
| Standalone MF | — | 0.03124894 | 94.31 |

The corrected MF baseline uses its earliest best-validation-RMSE checkpoint, epoch 4, with displayed validation RMSE 0.9779. This objective differs from PPR’s validation Recall@10 selection. The final comparison reused that trained checkpoint and cached validation PPR profiles, computing missing test profiles; nothing was refit on test. Global PageRank converged in 19 iterations (L1 residual 5.17×10⁻⁷); the displayed user-2 PPR run took 21 (9.93×10⁻⁷), not a cohort-wide maximum. Full precision and exclusions are in [results.csv](results/final_evaluation/results.csv) and [metrics.json](results/final_evaluation/metrics.json).

### 4.2 Fixed users, popularity evidence and one-factor changes

**Setup.**

Users A=1 and B=2 were fixed, and both belong to the common test cohort. User 1 has 217 training ratings, 131 positive; its positive history includes 61 Drama, 39 Comedy and 36 Action movies. User 2 has 49 training ratings, 32 positive, including 18 Drama and 11 each Romance and Comedy; genre counts overlap. These are historical ratings, not inferred current-session intent. [History evidence](report/user_histories.json).

**Results.**

Table 4. Final lists (PageRank/PPR α=0.50): mean popularity counts distinct positive-training users; overlap compares the two users within a method.

| Method | User 1 mean popularity | User 2 mean popularity | Shared movies / 10 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Popularity | 246.8 | 262.1 | 1 |
| Global PageRank | 239.4 | 247.4 | 1 |
| PPR | 228.4 | 226.7 | 1 |
| Standalone MF | 99.1 | 79.9 | 4 |

The [eight complete Top-10 lists](results/users_1_2/index.html) and [80-row CSV](results/users_1_2/recommendations.csv) include every ID, title, genres, score, training popularity and known test rating; unknown remains unobserved. For user 1, PPR starts with *Fargo* (Crime, Drama, Thriller), whereas MF starts with *The Wrong Trousers* (Animation, Comedy). For user 2, PPR starts with *Return of the Jedi* (Action, Adventure, Romance, Sci-Fi, War), whereas MF starts with *Persuasion* (Romance). These differences do not establish preference fit: user 2 has no Top-10 hits under any method. Both users receive ten positive-score candidates in all four methods.

Table 5. Required demonstrations, separate from final evaluation. All settings use the same training graph and standard per-user test filtering.

| Setting | User | α | Mean popularity | Overlap with setting 1 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1 | 0.85 | 245.5 | — |
| 2 | 2 | 0.85 | 254.9 | 0/10 |
| 3 | 1 | 0.50 | 228.4 | 7/10 |

Settings 1→2 change user at α=0.85: zero overlap, with mean popularity 245.5→254.9. All ten user-2 recommendations were already rated by user 1, and six user-1 recommendations were excluded for user 2, so the difference includes user-specific filtering. ## 5. Discussion

**Failure case.**

MF originally produced nearly identical predictions close to μ and poorly distinguished users and movies. The saved [failure record](results/mf_root_cause.json) preserves this symptom and the diagnosed loss definition.

**Root cause.**

MSE was averaged over the current mini-batch, while L2 was summed over every user and movie factor on every batch. At the configured coefficient, this scale imbalance suppressed factor learning, including factors unrelated to the current observations.

**Fix and verification.**

The loss now averages the squared norms of the user/movie rows gathered for current-batch observations: mean_batch(error²)+0.05·mean_batch(||pᵤ||²+||qᵢ||²), retaining repeated-observation weights. `hw6MfBatchLoss()` ([script.js:837](script.js#L837)) and its regression check show that unrelated rows neither change the loss nor receive gradients. The post-fix harness passes 21/0/0; epoch 4 is selected by validation RMSE. The retrieval comparison uses this corrected model, not the older collapsed model.

**What worked.**

- PPR has the highest observed common-cohort Recall@10, while the fixed-user and Fargo audits verify filtering and score interpretation.
- A lower α improves validation retrieval in this grid; the controlled user-1 example also reduces mean popularity, without proving that less popular recommendations are better.

Draft deployment interpretation for student review: replace the current MF baseline with PPR for the warm-user Top-10 surface, subject to an online test; this conclusion applies to this baseline and protocol, not all MF systems. Pair lists, multi-genre histories and popularity describe output differences, while cohort recall supplies the retrieval comparison. The per-user split, static explicit ratings and warm cohort cannot establish current-session intent, completion, retention, revenue or cold-start performance.

Before rollout, assign accounts persistently to MF control or PPR α=0.50 treatment, keeping interface, exposure and eligibility rules fixed. The proposed primary outcome is the fraction of exposed users starting a recommended movie and watching at least ten minutes within 24 hours; guardrails are total watch time per exposed user and p95 recommendation latency. Analyze at the assigned-user level without switching arms between sessions, and set the observation window and decision rule before examining results.

**What surprised me or did not work.**

- **Draft reflection, not yet student-confirmed:** fixing the loss made predictions distinguishable, but MF still had the lowest retrieval recall; improving an MSE-based learner does not guarantee better Top-10 ranking.
- Zero overlap for the two α=0.85 users is partly explained by exclusions. Neither that overlap nor the lower mean popularity of MF’s lists demonstrates superior personalization or discovery.

## 5. Discussion

**Failure case.**

MF originally produced nearly identical predictions close to μ and poorly distinguished users and movies. The saved [failure record](results/mf_root_cause.json) preserves this symptom and the diagnosed loss definition.

**Root cause.**

MSE was averaged over the current mini-batch, while L2 was summed over every user and movie factor on every batch. At the configured coefficient, this scale imbalance suppressed factor learning, including factors unrelated to the current observations.

**Fix and verification.**

The loss now averages the squared norms of the user/movie rows gathered for current-batch observations: mean_batch(error²)+0.05·mean_batch(||pᵤ||²+||qᵢ||²), retaining repeated-observation weights. `hw6MfBatchLoss()` ([script.js:837](script.js#L837)) and its regression check show that unrelated rows neither change the loss nor receive gradients. The post-fix harness passes 21/0/0; epoch 4 is selected by validation RMSE. The retrieval comparison uses this corrected model, not the older collapsed model.

**What worked.**

- PPR has the highest observed common-cohort Recall@10, while the fixed-user and Fargo audits verify filtering and score interpretation.
- A lower α improves validation retrieval in this grid; the controlled user-1 example also reduces mean popularity, without proving that less popular recommendations are better.

Draft deployment interpretation for student review: replace the current MF baseline with PPR for the warm-user Top-10 surface, subject to an online test; this conclusion applies to this baseline and protocol, not all MF systems. Pair lists, multi-genre histories and popularity describe output differences, while cohort recall supplies the retrieval comparison. The per-user split, static explicit ratings and warm cohort cannot establish current-session intent, completion, retention, revenue or cold-start performance.

Before rollout, assign accounts persistently to MF control or PPR α=0.50 treatment, keeping interface, exposure and eligibility rules fixed. The proposed primary outcome is the fraction of exposed users starting a recommended movie and watching at least ten minutes within 24 hours; guardrails are total watch time per exposed user and p95 recommendation latency. Analyze at the assigned-user level without switching arms between sessions, and set the observation window and decision rule before examining results.

**What surprised me or did not work.**

- **Draft reflection, not yet student-confirmed:** fixing the loss made predictions distinguishable, but MF still had the lowest retrieval recall; improving an MSE-based learner does not guarantee better Top-10 ranking.
- Zero overlap for the two α=0.85 users is partly explained by exclusions. Neither that overlap nor the lower mean popularity of MF’s lists demonstrates superior personalization or discovery.

# Personalized PageRank for MovieLens Top 10 Retrieval

**Student:** Raimova Alina  
**Team:** Individual  
**Email:** aaraimova@edu.hse.ru
**Date:** 2026-10-27  
**Assignment:** Graph-Based Recommendations with Personalized PageRank (Week 6, HW6)
**Github link:** [MOCK — repository URL to add]

## Abstract

This study tests whether Personalized PageRank can improve warm-user movie retrieval over popularity, global PageRank, and a matrix-factorization baseline on MovieLens 100K. The protocol uses 79,619 training, 9,596 validation, and 10,785 test ratings, mean training rating μ = 3.58060262, and popularity Recall@10 = 0.07602291. With alpha selected on validation, PPR reaches test Recall@10 of 0.11218853 across 861 common users, compared with 0.03124894 for the corrected MF baseline. These offline results support testing PPR as the warm-user Top-10 recommender, while leaving viewing and business outcomes to a user-level online experiment.

**Index Terms -** personalized PageRank, movie recommendation, matrix factorization, retrieval evaluation

## 1. Introduction

**Problem statement.**

The task ranks eligible unseen movies from explicit MovieLens ratings while treating missing entries as unobserved. It compares graph walks with popularity and the current standalone MF baseline under one shared retrieval protocol.

**Motivation.**

A rating predictor can have useful RMSE yet retrieve few held-out relevant movies. A consistent candidate pool, exclusion rule and warm-user cohort are therefore needed before choosing a Top-10 recommender.

**Concrete example.**

For user 1, Fargo was not rated in training or validation, so it can be recommended. The worked example traces its PPR score through normalization and checks its held-out rating of 5.

**Contributions.**

- Implement and verify TensorFlow.js PageRank/PPR, including equal outgoing probabilities, personal restart and dangling-mass preservation.
- Compare four methods with validation-selected settings, retain fixed-user evidence, and diagnose the MF regularization defect with a regression check.

## 2. Related Work

MovieLens documents explicit ratings and rating timestamps [1]. PageRank aggregates incoming link mass after dividing each source’s mass among its outgoing links [2]; personalized restart biases this process toward selected nodes [3]. MF estimates observed ratings using latent-factor interactions and regularization [4]. TensorFlow.js supplies the tensor operations and explicit memory management used here [5].

[1] F. M. Harper and J. A. Konstan, “The MovieLens Datasets: History and Context,” *ACM Transactions on Interactive Intelligent Systems*, vol. 5, no. 4, Art. 19, 2015, doi: 10.1145/2827872. [Publication record](https://experts.umn.edu/en/publications/the-movielens-datasets-history-and-context/); [official 100K README](https://files.grouplens.org/datasets/movielens/ml-100k/README). Accessed: Oct. 27, 2026.

[2] L. Page, S. Brin, R. Motwani, and T. Winograd, “The PageRank Citation Ranking: Bringing Order to the Web,” Stanford InfoLab, Technical Report, 1999. [Archived Stanford record](https://web.archive.org/web/20091118014915/http:/ilpubs.stanford.edu:8090/422/); [early draft dated Jan. 29, 1998](https://cs.brown.edu/courses/csci2531/papers/pagerank.pdf). Accessed: Oct. 27, 2026.

[3] G. Jeh and J. Widom, “Scaling personalized web search,” in *Proc. 12th Int. Conf. World Wide Web*, 2003, pp. 271–279, doi: 10.1145/775152.775191. [Conference full text](https://areto.ethz.ch/CDstore/www2003/papers/refereed/p185/html/p185-jeh.html). Accessed: Oct. 27, 2026.

[4] Y. Koren, R. Bell, and C. Volinsky, “Matrix Factorization Techniques for Recommender Systems,” *Computer*, vol. 42, no. 8, 2009, doi: 10.1109/MC.2009.263. [Primary article](https://www.cs.columbia.edu/~blei/fogm/readings/KorenBellVolinsky2009.pdf). Accessed: Oct. 27, 2026.

**Alternatives considered.**

- **Popularity and global PageRank:** retain transparent, nonpersonal baselines; global scores still receive each user’s exclusions.
- **MF:** retain an observed-rating latent-factor comparator; its checkpoint objective is rating error, unlike PPR’s retrieval objective.

## 3. Method

**Approach.**

Popularity counts distinct users with a training rating ≥4 per movie. Construct a binary bidirectional user–movie graph from those positive ratings. For nonzero-degree nodes, Q divides outgoing mass by degree; zero-degree rows remain zero. Iterate p₀=v and p(t+1)=α(Qᵀp(t)+d(t)v)+(1−α)v, where d(t) is dangling mass. Global PageRank uses uniform v; PPR uses one-hot restart at the target user, with α the link-following probability.

**Pipeline.**

1. Load `u.data` and Latin-1 `u.item`; split per user with `data.js`.
2. Build contiguous training-ID mappings and the positive graph; propagate with `R` and `Rᵀ` matrix blocks.
3. Select shared α on validation; restore MF’s validation-RMSE checkpoint.
4. Rank eligible training-movie candidates and evaluate the same test users.

**Tools and libraries.**

- TensorFlow.js **4.22.0**, **WebGL**, Float32: batched propagation and MF [5]; d3 **7.9.0**: graph display only. Python **3.12.14** and NumPy **2.3.5** provide independent numerical audits.
- `tf.tidy()` scopes synchronous steps; retained tensors are disposed. `dataSync()` readback and cooperative yields are used because asynchronous readback stalled this app; no async callback is placed inside `tidy`. Exact GPU/browser build and algorithm-only wall times were not recorded, so no speed benchmark is claimed.

**Key design decisions.**

- **Training-only graph:** 943 users + 1,611 movies = 2,554 nodes; 45,602 positive edges, one zero-degree user and 253 zero-degree movies. No graph/candidate padding node is added; low ratings are observed exclusions, not positive edges or missing zero targets.
- **Mass and convergence:** stop at L1 residual <10⁻⁶ or 500 iterations; report caps honestly. The batch width is 32, with columns frozen independently. Positive-user PPR corrects Float32 partition drift using analytically known finite-iteration user/movie totals before measuring residual.

**Configuration.**

MF scores are μ+pᵤᵀqᵢ, with 16 factors, seed 20261013, Adam learning rate 0.01, batch size 512, 30 epochs and L2 coefficient 0.05. Missing pairs are not rating targets. ## 5. Discussion

**Failure case.**

MF originally produced nearly identical predictions close to μ and poorly distinguished users and movies. The saved [failure record](results/mf_root_cause.json) preserves this symptom and the diagnosed loss definition.

**Root cause.**

MSE was averaged over the current mini-batch, while L2 was summed over every user and movie factor on every batch. At the configured coefficient, this scale imbalance suppressed factor learning, including factors unrelated to the current observations.

**Fix and verification.**

The loss now averages the squared norms of the user/movie rows gathered for current-batch observations: mean_batch(error²)+0.05·mean_batch(||pᵤ||²+||qᵢ||²), retaining repeated-observation weights. `hw6MfBatchLoss()` ([script.js:837](script.js#L837)) and its regression check show that unrelated rows neither change the loss nor receive gradients. The post-fix harness passes 21/0/0; epoch 4 is selected by validation RMSE. The retrieval comparison uses this corrected model, not the older collapsed model.

**What worked.**

- PPR has the highest observed common-cohort Recall@10, while the fixed-user and Fargo audits verify filtering and score interpretation.
- A lower α improves validation retrieval in this grid; the controlled user-1 example also reduces mean popularity, without proving that less popular recommendations are better.

Draft deployment interpretation for student review: replace the current MF baseline with PPR for the warm-user Top-10 surface, subject to an online test; this conclusion applies to this baseline and protocol, not all MF systems. Pair lists, multi-genre histories and popularity describe output differences, while cohort recall supplies the retrieval comparison. The per-user split, static explicit ratings and warm cohort cannot establish current-session intent, completion, retention, revenue or cold-start performance.

Before rollout, assign accounts persistently to MF control or PPR α=0.50 treatment, keeping interface, exposure and eligibility rules fixed. The proposed primary outcome is the fraction of exposed users starting a recommended movie and watching at least ten minutes within 24 hours; guardrails are total watch time per exposed user and p95 recommendation latency. Analyze at the assigned-user level without switching arms between sessions, and set the observation window and decision rule before examining results.

**What surprised me or did not work.**

- **Draft reflection, not yet student-confirmed:** fixing the loss made predictions distinguishable, but MF still had the lowest retrieval recall; improving an MSE-based learner does not guarantee better Top-10 ranking.
- Zero overlap for the two α=0.85 users is partly explained by exclusions. Neither that overlap nor the lower mean popularity of MF’s lists demonstrates superior personalization or discovery.

# Personalized PageRank for MovieLens Top 10 Retrieval

**Student:** Raimova Alina  
**Team:** Individual  
**Email:** aaraimova@edu.hse.ru
**Date:** 2026-10-27  
**Assignment:** Graph-Based Recommendations with Personalized PageRank (Week 6, HW6)
**Github link:** [MOCK — repository URL to add]

## Abstract

This study tests whether Personalized PageRank can improve warm-user movie retrieval over popularity, global PageRank, and a matrix-factorization baseline on MovieLens 100K. The protocol uses 79,619 training, 9,596 validation, and 10,785 test ratings, mean training rating μ = 3.58060262, and popularity Recall@10 = 0.07602291. With alpha selected on validation, PPR reaches test Recall@10 of 0.11218853 across 861 common users, compared with 0.03124894 for the corrected MF baseline. These offline results support testing PPR as the warm-user Top-10 recommender, while leaving viewing and business outcomes to a user-level online experiment.

**Index Terms -** personalized PageRank, movie recommendation, matrix factorization, retrieval evaluation

## 1. Introduction

**Problem statement.**

The task ranks eligible unseen movies from explicit MovieLens ratings while treating missing entries as unobserved. It compares graph walks with popularity and the current standalone MF baseline under one shared retrieval protocol.

**Motivation.**

A rating predictor can have useful RMSE yet retrieve few held-out relevant movies. A consistent candidate pool, exclusion rule and warm-user cohort are therefore needed before choosing a Top-10 recommender.

**Concrete example.**

For user 1, Fargo was not rated in training or validation, so it can be recommended. The worked example traces its PPR score through normalization and checks its held-out rating of 5.

**Contributions.**

- Implement and verify TensorFlow.js PageRank/PPR, including equal outgoing probabilities, personal restart and dangling-mass preservation.
- Compare four methods with validation-selected settings, retain fixed-user evidence, and diagnose the MF regularization defect with a regression check.

## 2. Related Work

MovieLens documents explicit ratings and rating timestamps [1]. PageRank aggregates incoming link mass after dividing each source’s mass among its outgoing links [2]; personalized restart biases this process toward selected nodes [3]. MF estimates observed ratings using latent-factor interactions and regularization [4]. TensorFlow.js supplies the tensor operations and explicit memory management used here [5].

[1] F. M. Harper and J. A. Konstan, “The MovieLens Datasets: History and Context,” *ACM Transactions on Interactive Intelligent Systems*, vol. 5, no. 4, Art. 19, 2015, doi: 10.1145/2827872. [Publication record](https://experts.umn.edu/en/publications/the-movielens-datasets-history-and-context/); [official 100K README](https://files.grouplens.org/datasets/movielens/ml-100k/README). Accessed: Oct. 27, 2026.

[2] L. Page, S. Brin, R. Motwani, and T. Winograd, “The PageRank Citation Ranking: Bringing Order to the Web,” Stanford InfoLab, Technical Report, 1999. [Archived Stanford record](https://web.archive.org/web/20091118014915/http:/ilpubs.stanford.edu:8090/422/); [early draft dated Jan. 29, 1998](https://cs.brown.edu/courses/csci2531/papers/pagerank.pdf). Accessed: Oct. 27, 2026.

[3] G. Jeh and J. Widom, “Scaling personalized web search,” in *Proc. 12th Int. Conf. World Wide Web*, 2003, pp. 271–279, doi: 10.1145/775152.775191. [Conference full text](https://areto.ethz.ch/CDstore/www2003/papers/refereed/p185/html/p185-jeh.html). Accessed: Oct. 27, 2026.

[4] Y. Koren, R. Bell, and C. Volinsky, “Matrix Factorization Techniques for Recommender Systems,” *Computer*, vol. 42, no. 8, 2009, doi: 10.1109/MC.2009.263. [Primary article](https://www.cs.columbia.edu/~blei/fogm/readings/KorenBellVolinsky2009.pdf). Accessed: Oct. 27, 2026.

[5] TensorFlow, “Tensors and operations,” *TensorFlow.js Guide*, and “TensorFlow.js API, version 4.22.0.” [Tensor guide](https://www.tensorflow.org/js/guide/tensors_operations); [versioned API](https://js.tensorflow.org/api/4.22.0/#tidy). Accessed: Oct. 27, 2026.

**Alternatives considered.**

- **Popularity and global PageRank:** retain transparent, nonpersonal baselines; global scores still receive each user’s exclusions.
- **MF:** retain an observed-rating latent-factor comparator; its checkpoint objective is rating error, unlike PPR’s retrieval objective.

## 3. Method

**Approach.**

Popularity counts distinct users with a training rating ≥4 per movie. Construct a binary bidirectional user–movie graph from those positive ratings. For nonzero-degree nodes, Q divides outgoing mass by degree; zero-degree rows remain zero. Iterate p₀=v and p(t+1)=α(Qᵀp(t)+d(t)v)+(1−α)v, where d(t) is dangling mass. Global PageRank uses uniform v; PPR uses one-hot restart at the target user, with α the link-following probability.

**Pipeline.**

1. Load `u.data` and Latin-1 `u.item`; split per user with `data.js`.
2. Build contiguous training-ID mappings and the positive graph; propagate with `R` and `Rᵀ` matrix blocks.
3. Select shared α on validation; restore MF’s validation-RMSE checkpoint.
4. Rank eligible training-movie candidates and evaluate the same test users.

**Tools and libraries.**

- TensorFlow.js **4.22.0**, **WebGL**, Float32: batched propagation and MF [5]; d3 **7.9.0**: graph display only. Python **3.12.14** and NumPy **2.3.5** provide independent numerical audits.
- `tf.tidy()` scopes synchronous steps; retained tensors are disposed. `dataSync()` readback and cooperative yields are used because asynchronous readback stalled this app; no async callback is placed inside `tidy`. Exact GPU/browser build and algorithm-only wall times were not recorded, so no speed benchmark is claimed.

**Key design decisions.**

- **Training-only graph:** 943 users + 1,611 movies = 2,554 nodes; 45,602 positive edges, one zero-degree user and 253 zero-degree movies. No graph/candidate padding node is added; low ratings are observed exclusions, not positive edges or missing zero targets.
- **Mass and convergence:** stop at L1 residual <10⁻⁶ or 500 iterations; report caps honestly. The batch width is 32, with columns frozen independently. Positive-user PPR corrects Float32 partition drift using analytically known finite-iteration user/movie totals before measuring residual.

**Configuration.**

Table 1. Data and popularity baseline, before model metrics; [full provenance](results/report_preamble.json).

| Required pre-model quantity | Value | Calculation source and settings |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Train / validation / test ratings | 79,619 / 9,596 / 10,785 | [data.js:145](data.js#L145), `splitByTimestamp()`; per-user floor(80%)/floor(10%)/remainder, timestamp then movie ID, minimum 5 ratings |
| μ, mean training rating | 3.58060261998 = 285,084 / 79,619 | [script.js:948](script.js#L948), mean inside `hw6TrainMf()`; all observed training ratings 1–5 only |
| Popularity baseline TEST Recall@10 | 0.07602291344 | [script.js:1250](script.js#L1250), `recallAtK("popularity",10,"test")`; 861 users, 1,611 candidates, relevance ≥4, training+validation exclusions |

The loaded data contain 100,000 ratings, 943 users and 1,682 metadata movies. Sparsity over the unpadded observed-ID rectangle is 93.6953%; training contains only 1,611 movies. No users are skipped at splitting. This is per-user chronological, not globally time-consistent; rating times are not viewing sessions.

MF scores are μ+pᵤᵀqᵢ, with 16 factors, seed 20261013, Adam learning rate 0.01, batch size 512, 30 epochs and L2 coefficient 0.05. Missing pairs are not rating targets. No completed Week-5 checkpoint is available, so this is an explicitly disclosed standalone-baseline deviation from the requested reuse. PPR has no optimizer or random seed; α∈{0.50,0.70,0.85,0.95} is selected on validation only. Scores are walk probabilities, not ratings or purchase probabilities, and are not comparable in scale with MF. Run: from `week6`, execute `python3 -m http.server 8000`, open `http://localhost:8000/index.html`, then use “Evaluate Recall@10 — all four methods”; the separate two-user demo is not part of that evaluation.

## 4. Experiments

### 4.1 Validation selection and final shared-cohort evaluation

**Setup.**

The candidate pool contains all 1,611 training movies. Validation excludes training-rated movies; test excludes every training- or validation-rated movie regardless of rating. Relevant items have evaluation rating ≥4 and remain eligible. Sort descending by score, breaking exact ties by ascending movie ID. Recall@10 is the macro-average of each user’s hits divided by eligible relevant items. Warm users need a positive training edge, scoreable MF candidates and eligible relevant held-out items. Validation has 846 users; test has 861 of 943. The 82 users without eligible relevant test items include the one zero-positive-edge user; these counts overlap. Thirteen relevant test observations are outside the candidate pool. Validation excludes 97 users without eligible relevance and four out-of-pool relevant observations.

**Results.**

Table 2. PPR validation selection; α = 0.50 wins, with exact ties assigned to the smaller α.

| α | Validation Recall@10 | Max iterations | All converged |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0.50 | 0.11448316 | 22 | yes |
| 0.70 | 0.10479695 | 42 | yes |
| 0.85 | 0.09002077 | 92 | yes |
| 0.95 | 0.07375030 | 287 | yes |

Table 3. Final TEST results on the same 861 users. The selected α also controls global PageRank; it was not separately optimized for PageRank.

| Method | α | Test Recall@10 | Mean training popularity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Popularity | — | 0.07602291 | 272.00 |
| Global PageRank | 0.50 | 0.07969324 | 257.82 |
| PPR | 0.50 | 0.11218853 | 244.21 |
| Standalone MF | — | 0.03124894 | 94.31 |

The corrected MF baseline uses its earliest best-validation-RMSE checkpoint, epoch 4, with displayed validation RMSE 0.9779. This objective differs from PPR’s validation Recall@10 selection. The final comparison reused that trained checkpoint and cached validation PPR profiles, computing missing test profiles; nothing was refit on test. Global PageRank converged in 19 iterations (L1 residual 5.17×10⁻⁷); the displayed user-2 PPR run took 21 (9.93×10⁻⁷), not a cohort-wide maximum. Full precision and exclusions are in [results.csv](results/final_evaluation/results.csv) and [metrics.json](results/final_evaluation/metrics.json).

### 4.2 Fixed users, popularity evidence and one-factor changes

**Setup.**

Users A=1 and B=2 were fixed, and both belong to the common test cohort. User 1 has 217 training ratings, 131 positive; its positive history includes 61 Drama, 39 Comedy and 36 Action movies. User 2 has 49 training ratings, 32 positive, including 18 Drama and 11 each Romance and Comedy; genre counts overlap. These are historical ratings, not inferred current-session intent. [History evidence](report/user_histories.json).

**Results.**

Table 4. Final lists (PageRank/PPR α=0.50): mean popularity counts distinct positive-training users; overlap compares the two users within a method.

| Method | User 1 mean popularity | User 2 mean popularity | Shared movies / 10 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Popularity | 246.8 | 262.1 | 1 |
| Global PageRank | 239.4 | 247.4 | 1 |
| PPR | 228.4 | 226.7 | 1 |
| Standalone MF | 99.1 | 79.9 | 4 |

The [eight complete Top-10 lists](results/users_1_2/index.html) and [80-row CSV](results/users_1_2/recommendations.csv) include every ID, title, genres, score, training popularity and known test rating; unknown remains unobserved. For user 1, PPR starts with *Fargo* (Crime, Drama, Thriller), whereas MF starts with *The Wrong Trousers* (Animation, Comedy). For user 2, PPR starts with *Return of the Jedi* (Action, Adventure, Romance, Sci-Fi, War), whereas MF starts with *Persuasion* (Romance). These differences do not establish preference fit: user 2 has no Top-10 hits under any method. Both users receive ten positive-score candidates in all four methods.

Table 5. Required demonstrations, separate from final evaluation. All settings use the same training graph and standard per-user test filtering.

| Setting | User | α | Mean popularity | Overlap with setting 1 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1 | 0.85 | 245.5 | — |
| 2 | 2 | 0.85 | 254.9 | 0/10 |
| 3 | 1 | 0.50 | 228.4 | 7/10 |

Settings 1→2 change user at α=0.85: zero overlap, with mean popularity 245.5→254.9. All ten user-2 recommendations were already rated by user 1, and six user-1 recommendations were excluded for user 2, so the difference includes user-specific filtering. Settings 1→3 hold user 1 and exclusions fixed and lower α from 0.85 to 0.50: seven shared movies, mean popularity 245.5→228.4. *Scream*, *Air Force One* and *Titanic* leave; *Trainspotting*, *Sense and Sensibility* and *E.T.* enter. Here higher α gives the more popular list; no universal novelty or quality improvement follows. [Three full lists and comparisons](results/ppr_demonstration/index.html).

### 4.3 Worked numerical verification for user 1 and Fargo

**Setup.**

For movie 100 at α=0.50, the original 32-column WebGL batch and a read-only observed copy were run on the same graph. User 1 maps to node 0; Fargo to node 1042, with 377 positive-training neighbours. The last update is iteration 21, residual 9.95331675×10⁻⁷. Incoming mass is the Float32 matrix reduction of neighbour probabilities divided across their degrees. Restart is at user 1, so Fargo’s restart entry is zero; total dangling mass is also zero. Sources: [graph.js:656](graph.js#L656) through its restart update, and [graphCorrectPartitionMass(), graph.js:730](graph.js#L730).

**Results.**

Table 6. Measured final-step values.

| Final-iteration value | Actual output |
| --- | --- |
| Incoming mass at Fargo | 0.0013710429193452 |
| Dangling / restart contribution at Fargo | 0 / 0 |
| Raw Fargo score = 0.50 × incoming | 0.0006855214596726 |
| Raw movie-partition sum | 0.3333335220813751 |
| Target movie-partition mass | 0.33333349227905273 |
| Final normalized Fargo score | 0.0006855214014649391 |
| Difference from saved score | 0 |

The actual correction is Float32(Float32(raw / 0.3333335220813751) × 0.33333349227905273), giving exactly **0.0006855214014649391**, the saved score. It lowers raw by 5.82076609×10⁻¹¹. The finite-iteration user target is (1+α(−α)ᵗ)/(1+α); movie target is its complement. The observed and original solver outputs match exactly across all 32 probability columns. A separate Float64 iteration gives 0.000685520996303016, a −4.05161923×10⁻¹⁰ precision difference, disclosed rather than substituted for the production value.

Fargo is in the training candidate pool but absent from user 1’s training and validation histories. It ranks first among 1,367 eligible candidates; its held-out rating is 5 ([u.data:17673](u.data#L17673)). All three Top-10 hits are:

| Rank | Movie ID | Top-10 hit | Test rating |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 100 | Fargo (1996) | 5 |
| 2 | 258 | Contact (1997) | 5 |
| 7 | 222 | Star Trek: First Contact (1996) | 4 |

User 1 has **19 eligible relevant test movies**, with IDs 6, 18, 20, 32, 100, 111, 129, 154, 169, 171, 178, 209, 221, 222, 228, 242, 256, 258 and 270; the other nine test ratings are below 4. Thus individual **Recall@10 = 3/19 = 0.1578947368**, distinct from the cohort average. [Complete explanation](results/user1_fargo_worked/index.html), [19-item audit](results/user1_fargo_worked/eligible_relevant_test_movies.csv) and [machine-readable vectors and contributions](results/user1_fargo_worked/intermediates.json) preserve exact values, source lines and numerical-rounding differences.

### 4.4 Verification coverage

**Setup.**

The post-fix harness covers reference vectors, normalized rows, restart validity, mass/nonnegativity, matrix orientation, dangling nodes, mapped seeds, caps, repeat-run memory, candidate filtering, macro recall, batched parity and the MF-loss regression. Sources: `runSelfChecks()` and `hw6CheckBatchedPpr()` in `script.js`.

**Results.**

The post-fix execution recorded **21 PASS, 0 FAIL, 0 PENDING** ([verification.json](results/final_evaluation/verification.json)). Twelve batch user/α fixture cases match single-user PPR; dangling restart and cleanup pass. Six propagation runs retain 2/2 live tensors in the MF-loaded harness; the separate Fargo trace has 0/0. All four validation sweeps converge within the cap. Checks establish implementation consistency, not user satisfaction or cold-start performance.

## 5. Discussion

**Failure case.**

MF originally produced nearly identical predictions close to μ and poorly distinguished users and movies. The saved [failure record](results/mf_root_cause.json) preserves this symptom and the diagnosed loss definition.

**Root cause.**

MSE was averaged over the current mini-batch, while L2 was summed over every user and movie factor on every batch. At the configured coefficient, this scale imbalance suppressed factor learning, including factors unrelated to the current observations.

**Fix and verification.**

The loss now averages the squared norms of the user/movie rows gathered for current-batch observations: mean_batch(error²)+0.05·mean_batch(||pᵤ||²+||qᵢ||²), retaining repeated-observation weights. `hw6MfBatchLoss()` ([script.js:837](script.js#L837)) and its regression check show that unrelated rows neither change the loss nor receive gradients. The post-fix harness passes 21/0/0; epoch 4 is selected by validation RMSE. The retrieval comparison uses this corrected model, not the older collapsed model.

**What worked.**

- PPR has the highest observed common-cohort Recall@10, while the fixed-user and Fargo audits verify filtering and score interpretation.
- A lower α improves validation retrieval in this grid; the controlled user-1 example also reduces mean popularity, without proving that less popular recommendations are better.

Draft deployment interpretation for student review: replace the current MF baseline with PPR for the warm-user Top-10 surface, subject to an online test; this conclusion applies to this baseline and protocol, not all MF systems. Pair lists, multi-genre histories and popularity describe output differences, while cohort recall supplies the retrieval comparison. The per-user split, static explicit ratings and warm cohort cannot establish current-session intent, completion, retention, revenue or cold-start performance.

Before rollout, assign accounts persistently to MF control or PPR α=0.50 treatment, keeping interface, exposure and eligibility rules fixed. The proposed primary outcome is the fraction of exposed users starting a recommended movie and watching at least ten minutes within 24 hours; guardrails are total watch time per exposed user and p95 recommendation latency. Analyze at the assigned-user level without switching arms between sessions, and set the observation window and decision rule before examining results.

**What surprised me or did not work.**

- **Draft reflection, not yet student-confirmed:** fixing the loss made predictions distinguishable, but MF still had the lowest retrieval recall; improving an MSE-based learner does not guarantee better Top-10 ranking.
- Zero overlap for the two α=0.85 users is partly explained by exclusions. Neither that overlap nor the lower mean popularity of MF’s lists demonstrates superior personalization or discovery.

- **How AI was used:** AI assisted data preparation, graph/propagation and retrieval implementation, MF debugging, numerical tracing, literature verification and report drafting; saved JSON/CSV artifacts preserve the outputs used here.

text(await tools.exec_command({cmd:"python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
p = Path('llm-4-res-sys/week6/student_hw6_report.md')
original = p.read_text()
metadata = original.split('## Abstract', 1)[0]
body = '''## Abstract

This study tests whether Personalized PageRank can improve warm-user movie retrieval over popularity, global PageRank, and a matrix-factorization baseline on MovieLens 100K. The protocol uses 79,619 training, 9,596 validation, and 10,785 test ratings, mean training rating μ = 3.58060262, and popularity Recall@10 = 0.07602291. With alpha selected on validation, PPR reaches test Recall@10 of 0.11218853 across 861 common users, compared with 0.03124894 for the corrected MF baseline. These offline results support testing PPR as the warm-user Top-10 recommender, while leaving viewing and business outcomes to a user-level online experiment.

**Index Terms -** personalized PageRank, movie recommendation, matrix factorization, retrieval evaluation

## 1. Introduction

**Problem statement.**

Rank unseen movies from explicit ratings, treating missing ratings as unobserved, and compare popularity, global PageRank, PPR and MF under the same retrieval protocol.

**Motivation.**

Low rating-prediction error does not guarantee useful Top-10 recommendations. Fair comparison requires common candidates, exclusions and evaluation users.

**Concrete example.**

User 1 has not rated Fargo in training or validation. PPR ranks it first, and its held-out test rating of 5 makes it a hit.

**Contributions.**

- Implement and verify PageRank/PPR with equal outgoing probabilities, personalized restart and dangling-mass handling.
- Compare four methods, trace one recommendation numerically, and diagnose and fix MF regularization.

## 2. Related Work

MovieLens provides explicit ratings and timestamps [1]. PageRank redistributes probability through links [2]; personalized restart makes the distribution depend on a selected user [3]. MF models observed ratings through latent factors [4]. TensorFlow.js provides the tensor operations and memory management used here [5].

[1] F. M. Harper and J. A. Konstan, “The MovieLens Datasets: History and Context,” *ACM Transactions on Interactive Intelligent Systems*, vol. 5, no. 4, Art. 19, 2015, doi: 10.1145/2827872.

[2] L. Page, S. Brin, R. Motwani, and T. Winograd, “The PageRank Citation Ranking: Bringing Order to the Web,” Stanford InfoLab, Technical Report, 1999.

[3] G. Jeh and J. Widom, “Scaling personalized web search,” in *Proc. 12th Int. Conf. World Wide Web*, 2003, pp. 271–279, doi: 10.1145/775152.775191.

[4] Y. Koren, R. Bell, and C. Volinsky, “Matrix Factorization Techniques for Recommender Systems,” *Computer*, vol. 42, no. 8, 2009, doi: 10.1109/MC.2009.263.

[5] TensorFlow, “Tensors and operations,” *TensorFlow.js Guide*, and *TensorFlow.js API*, version 4.22.0. Accessed: Oct. 27, 2026.

**Alternatives considered.**

Popularity and global PageRank provide nonpersonal baselines. MF provides an observed-rating predictor whose validation objective differs from PPR’s retrieval objective.

## 3. Method

**Approach.**

Build a binary bidirectional user–movie graph from training ratings ≥4. For a node with degree d, each outgoing link has probability 1/d; dangling rows are zero. Starting with p₀=v, update

p(t+1) = α[Qᵀp(t) + d(t)v] + (1−α)v,

where Q contains outgoing probabilities and d(t) is total dangling mass. Global PageRank uses uniform restart v; PPR restarts at the chosen user. Thus α follows links and 1−α restarts. Popularity counts distinct users with positive training ratings.

**Pipeline.**

1. Load ratings and movie metadata; split each user’s ratings chronologically.
2. Build the training graph and train MF on observed ratings.
3. Select α on validation and restore MF’s best validation-RMSE checkpoint.
4. Exclude previously rated movies, rank candidates and evaluate the common test cohort.

**Tools and libraries.**

TensorFlow.js 4.22.0 runs Float32 calculations on WebGL; d3 7.9.0 displays the graph. Python 3.12.14 and NumPy 2.3.5 support independent numerical audits. Tensor scopes and explicit disposal manage memory; cooperative yields keep batch computation responsive. Hardware details and isolated algorithm timings were not recorded.

**Key design decisions.**

- The training graph contains 943 users and 1,611 movies: 2,554 nodes and 45,602 positive edges. One user and 253 movies have no positive links. Missing ratings are never zero-valued targets.
- Stop when the L1 residual is below 10⁻⁶, with a 500-iteration cap. Batched PPR uses 32 columns with independent stopping. A finite-iteration partition correction controls Float32 mass drift.

**Configuration.**

Table 1. Data and popularity baseline before model metrics. Source names identify the calculations; the essential values and settings are included here.

| Quantity | Value | Calculation and settings |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Train / validation / test ratings | 79,619 / 9,596 / 10,785 | `data.js`, `splitByTimestamp()`: per user, timestamp then movie ID; floor(80%), floor(10%), remainder; minimum 5 ratings |
| Training mean μ | 3.58060261998 = 285,084 / 79,619 | `script.js`, `hw6TrainMf()`: mean of all observed training ratings |
| Popularity test Recall@10 | 0.07602291344 | `script.js`, `recallAtK("popularity",10,"test")`: relevance ≥4, training+validation exclusions, 861 users |

MovieLens contains 100,000 ratings, 943 users and 1,682 metadata movies; no users are skipped. Sparsity is 93.6953% over the unpadded user–movie rectangle. The split is chronological within users, rather than globally chronological.

MF predicts μ+pᵤᵀqᵢ using 16 factors, seed 20261013, Adam learning rate 0.01, batch size 512, 30 epochs and L2 coefficient 0.05. A completed Week-5 checkpoint was unavailable, so the implemented standalone baseline is a deviation from requested reuse. PPR selects α from {0.50, 0.70, 0.85, 0.95}. Its probability scores and MF’s rating predictions have different scales.

## 4. Experiments

### 4.1 Validation selection and final evaluation

**Setup.**

Candidates are the 1,611 training movies. Validation excludes all training-rated movies; test excludes all training- and validation-rated movies, regardless of rating. Relevant held-out ratings are ≥4 and eligible. Rank by descending score, breaking ties by ascending movie ID. Recall@10 averages each user’s hits divided by eligible relevant movies.

The shared warm cohort contains 846 validation users and 861 test users. Eighty-two users lack eligible relevant test movies, including the isolated user; 13 relevant test observations fall outside the candidate pool. MF is scoreable on the same candidates.

**Results.**

Table 2. Validation sweep; all runs converge. Select α=0.50, using smaller α for exact ties.

| α | Validation Recall@10 | Maximum iterations |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0.50 | 0.11448316 | 22 |
| 0.70 | 0.10479695 | 42 |
| 0.85 | 0.09002077 | 92 |
| 0.95 | 0.07375030 | 287 |

Table 3. Final test comparison on the same 861 users. Mean popularity counts positive-training users per recommended movie.

| Method | α | Test Recall@10 | Mean popularity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Popularity | — | 0.07602291 | 272.00 |
| Global PageRank | 0.50 | 0.07969324 | 257.82 |
| PPR | 0.50 | 0.11218853 | 244.21 |
| Standalone MF | — | 0.03124894 | 94.31 |

Global PageRank uses the PPR-selected α and was not separately optimized. MF uses the earliest best-validation-RMSE checkpoint, epoch 4, with displayed validation RMSE 0.9779. Neither model was refit on test. PPR has the highest observed recall; MF’s lower popularity does not establish better recommendations.

### 4.2 Fixed-user lists and controlled PPR demonstrations

**Setup.**

Fix A=1 and B=2; both belong to the common test cohort. User 1 has 217 training ratings, 131 positive, and 19 eligible relevant test movies. User 2 has 49 training ratings, 32 positive, and two eligible relevant test movies. Generate eight final Top-10 lists using the selected α and standard test filtering; missing held-out ratings remain unknown.

**Results.**

Table 4. Final lists: mean popularity and the number of shared movies between users.

| Method | User 1 mean popularity | User 2 mean popularity | Shared / 10 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Popularity | 246.8 | 262.1 | 1 |
| Global PageRank | 239.4 | 247.4 | 1 |
| PPR | 228.4 | 226.7 | 1 |
| MF | 99.1 | 79.9 | 4 |

PPR starts with *Fargo* (Crime, Drama, Thriller) for user 1 and *Return of the Jedi* (Action, Adventure, Romance, Sci-Fi, War) for user 2. MF starts with *The Wrong Trousers* (Animation, Comedy) and *Persuasion* (Romance), respectively. User 2 has no Top-10 hits under any method.

Table 5. Demonstrations using the same training graph, kept separate from final evaluation.

| Setting | User | α | Mean popularity | Overlap with setting 1 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1 | 0.85 | 245.5 | — |
| 2 | 2 | 0.85 | 254.9 | 0/10 |
| 3 | 1 | 0.50 | 228.4 | 7/10 |

Changing the user at α=0.85 gives zero overlap, partly because exclusions differ: all ten user-2 recommendations were already rated by user 1. Lowering α for user 1 preserves seven movies: *Scream*, *Air Force One* and *Titanic* leave; *Trainspotting*, *Sense and Sensibility* and *E.T.* enter. Higher α produces the more popular list in this example; this is not a universal quality or popularity rule.

### 4.3 Worked example: user 1, Fargo, α=0.50

**Setup.**

Fargo (movie 100) has 377 positive-training neighbours. In iteration 21, the final L1 residual is 9.95331675×10⁻⁷. Incoming mass is the sum of neighbouring probabilities divided by their degrees. Fargo receives no direct restart contribution because restart is at user 1; total dangling mass is zero. The update and correction are implemented in `graph.js`, including `graphCorrectPartitionMass()`.

**Results.**

Table 6. Actual final-iteration Float32 values.

| Component | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Incoming mass at Fargo | 0.0013710429193452 |
| Dangling contribution | 0 |
| Restart contribution | 0 |
| Raw score: 0.50 × incoming | 0.0006855214596726 |
| Raw movie-partition mass | 0.3333335220813751 |
| Target movie-partition mass | 0.33333349227905273 |
| Final score | 0.0006855214014649391 |
| Difference from saved score | 0 |

The numerical correction is Float32(Float32(raw / 0.3333335220813751) × 0.33333349227905273). It reduces the raw score by 5.82076609×10⁻¹¹. The user-partition target at iteration t is (1+α(−α)ᵗ)/(1+α); the movie target is its complement. Original and observed batch outputs match exactly. An independent Float64 solver gives 0.000685520996303016, differing by −4.05161923×10⁻¹⁰ through numerical precision.

Fargo is absent from user 1’s training and validation histories, is eligible, and ranks **1st of 1,367 candidates**. Its held-out test rating in `u.data` is **5**. The three Top-10 hits are:

| Rank | Movie ID | Title | Test rating |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 100 | Fargo (1996) | 5 |
| 2 | 258 | Contact (1997) | 5 |
| 7 | 222 | Star Trek: First Contact (1996) | 4 |

The 19 eligible relevant test IDs are 6, 18, 20, 32, 100, 111, 129, 154, 169, 171, 178, 209, 221, 222, 228, 242, 256, 258 and 270. The remaining nine test ratings are below 4. Therefore user-1 **Recall@10 = 3/19 = 0.1578947**, distinct from cohort recall. Filtering, ranking and recall use `script.js`, including `recallAtK()`.

### 4.4 Implementation verification

**Setup.**

`runSelfChecks()` and `hw6CheckBatchedPpr()` cover transition normalization, restart, dangling nodes, probability mass, convergence, candidate filtering, macro recall, batch parity, tensor cleanup and the MF-loss regression.

**Results.**

The recorded post-fix harness reports **21 PASS, 0 FAIL, 0 PENDING**. Twelve user/α fixture cases match single-user PPR. Six repeated propagation runs retain 2/2 live tensors with MF loaded; the separate Fargo trace retains 0/0. All four validation sweeps converge within the cap.

## 5. Discussion

**Failure case.**

MF initially produced nearly identical predictions close to the global mean μ, poorly distinguishing users and movies.

**Root cause.**

MSE was averaged over the current mini-batch, while L2 was summed over all user and movie factors on every batch. At the configured coefficient, this imbalance suppressed factor learning.

**Fix and verification.**

`hw6MfBatchLoss()` now averages L2 over factor rows gathered for the current batch, retaining repeated-observation weights:

loss = mean(error²) + 0.05 × mean(‖pᵤ‖² + ‖qᵢ‖²).

Unrelated factor rows no longer alter the loss or receive gradients. The regression check passes within the 21/0/0 harness. All reported final MF metrics use the corrected model.

**What worked.**

PPR achieves the highest common-cohort recall, supported by the explicit Fargo calculation. Draft interpretation for student review: test PPR against this MF baseline for warm-user Top-10 retrieval. This finding concerns the implemented baseline and protocol, not all MF models.

Before deployment, assign accounts persistently to MF control or PPR α=0.50 treatment with the same interface and eligibility. A proposed primary outcome is the fraction of exposed users starting a recommendation and watching at least ten minutes within 24 hours; monitor total watch time and p95 recommendation latency. Fix the observation window and decision rule in advance.

**What surprised me or did not work.**

Draft reflection, pending student review: correcting MF’s loss did not make it competitive on retrieval recall. Low list popularity and low overlap alone do not prove useful personalization. Static ratings, per-user chronology and a warm cohort cannot establish current intent, online engagement or cold-start performance.

## 6. AI Usage Disclosure

- **AI tools used:** OpenAI Codex with browser/terminal tools and a reference-verification sub-agent; exact model/build was not recorded.
- **How AI was used:** Implementation, debugging, numerical checks, literature verification and report drafting.
- **What I personally verified:** Student verification is not confirmed; the reported computational checks were performed by the agent.
- **What I trusted without full verification:** Student statement and interpretation remain pending review. The GitHub field remains a mock placeholder.
- **Session log reference:** The required authentic, unmodified `student_hw6_session.json` has not been supplied; no synthetic log was created.

## References

See §2 (numbered [1]–[5]).
'''
p.write_text(metadata + body)
print('Updated', p)
print('Whitespace words:', len((metadata + body).split()))
PY","max_output_tokens":500}));

# OpenAI Docs

Provide current, cited OpenAI product, API, model, and Codex guidance. Read zero or one primary reference.

**First substantive action:** Search the user's exact requested official OpenAI documentation topic and any explicitly named model using a concise, topic-specific query of 2-6 essential terms. When an already-available direct official documentation search and page-retrieval capability is present, use it first: search, then fetch or open the matching official page before general web search. Otherwise, immediately use official-domain web search, then actually open or fetch the relevant official page. Complete this source order before reading a reference, inspecting local or repository files, running a Codex manual or model resolver, drafting a plan, or answering from memory. Use the actual fetched page, not a search snippet or an unopened link. If one official search or page does not establish the answer, search another appropriate official domain and actually open or fetch the result. Preserve the exact requested model; never substitute a newer model.

**Only exception:** An explicitly requested, genuinely broad, cross-topic Codex setup, orientation, or system-map synthesis may use the manual first when shell execution and an allowed temporary cache are available. A specific Codex feature, setting, command, error, model, or requested citation remains docs-first. Mixed Chat/Work/Codex comparisons are official documentation questions, not manual-first Codex requests.

For generic software tasks, answer the software task directly. OpenAI implementation, debugging, SDK, API, prompting, agent, and eval requests are not generic.

For a straightforward factual or citation-only request, follow the source order and do not read a route reference. This includes straightforward API facts, ChatGPT Work or mixed Chat/Work/Codex comparisons, model tiers, aliases, Pro mode, reasoning settings, factual migration baselines, and narrow Codex facts. Prioritize `learn.chatgpt.com` for ChatGPT Work.

## Choose one primary route

Use the first matching route, and read its reference only when the requested task needs that specialized workflow:

- **Explicitly requested local documentation integration:** Read [integration guidance](references/mcp-diagnostics.md) only when the user explicitly requests that local integration.
